newsitem.title: FRANCE: Far-right could capture fourth French town in vote.
newsitem.headline: Far-right could capture fourth French town in vote.

text.p: With the whole of France watching, Jean-Marie Le Pen's extreme-right National Front party has a strong chance of capturing a fourth southern French town on Sunday in the runoff of a municipal election in Vitrolles.

The depressed satellite town of 40,000 residents north of Marseille became the centre of French politics this week as national leaders of the Left poured in to try to save unpopular Socialist mayor Jean-Jacques Anglade from defeat at the hands of Catherine Megret, wife of the Front's number two.

Megret won 46.7 percent of the vote in last Sunday's first round, boosting the anti-immigration movement's score by four points since 1995, after a court disqualified her husband, Bruno, for campaign spending irregularities.
Anglade, who won re-election by a mere 353 votes in 1995, took 37 percent last Sunday at the head of a united list of Socialists, Communists and ecologists on a 76 percent turnout.

Conservative candidate Roger Guichard scored 16.3 percent and pulled out of the second ballot at the insistence of Prime Minister Alain Juppe's centre-right national coalition urging a "republican vote to bar the road to the extreme-right".
National centre-right leaders have stayed away from Vitrolles and it is far from certain their voters will switch to Anglade, whom they accuse of bankrupting the drab town.
In separate eleventh-hour complaints on Friday, both Anglade and Guichard asked a Marseille court to annul the first round result.
Anglade accused Catherine Megret of spending 1.2 million francs ($210,000), three times the permitted sum, and of offences including "defamation, insults, threats and incitement to racial hatred".
Guichard also alleged he had been defamed, and complained ballots in the name of Megret failed to bear the required mention of the Republic's motto "Liberty, Equality, Fraternity".

The Front said Anglade was desperate and branded his attacks ridiculous. "He's behaving as if he's already lost," said Bruno Megret, saying Anglade's local supporters were responsible for intimidation, defamation and attacks on Front members.
If Megret wins, Vitrolles will be the fourth town it controls after a breakthrough in 1995 when it captured Toulon, Orange and Marignane, all in the south of France.

Socialist leader Lionel Jospin, Communist leader Robert Hue and Radical Socialist ex-minister Bernard Kouchner, flanked by film stars and Jewish community leaders, appealed to Vitrolles citizens on Wednesday to vote against "racism and hatred".
But Socialist officials privately acknowledge that Anglade, under judicial investigation for alleged sleaze, is a poor advertisement for a party keen to shake off past graft scandals.

Bruno Megret, who plans to be his wife's chief aide if she wins, hammered home charges that France's political class is corrupt and told some 1,500 supporters at a final rally on Thursday they could be proud of their vote "which impressed the whole of Europe".

"I read that it was a disgrace, that the town and democracy are supposedly in danger. The Parisians have no place teaching us lessons," he declared to cheers. Even so, the Megrets do not have a vote in Vitrolles because they are resident near Paris.
Sticking to a local strategy, Megret did not invite Le Pen to Vitrolles during the campaign.

The Front, which has played up the law-and-order issue in Vitrolles, advocates expelling some three million immigrants from France and giving preference in housing, jobs and welfare benefits to French nationals.

Unemployment, well above the 12.7 percent national average, is a big factor in Vitrolles. The high-rise town was started in the 1970s to house workers drawn by an ambitious steelworks complex in Fos-sur-Mer which foundered.
